extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and applicants concerned with §101 subject-matter eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Performing the U.S. patent eligibility analysis under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the USPTO/MPEP workflow: Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (Prong One: identify judicial exceptions; Prong Two: integration into a practical application), and Step 2B (significantly more/inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must be to a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.03 for how courts have defined the four categories, examples of subject matter that does not fall within any category (e.g., software per se, signals per se, human organisms), and guidance on evaluating whether the claimed invention fits a statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One: Abstract ideas (identify judicial exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites an abstract idea by evaluating whether claim limitation(s) fall within at least one of three groupings of abstract ideas: mathematical concepts; mental processes; and certain methods of organizing human activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.04(a). Use examples (e.g., Training a Neural Network Example 39; Livestock Management Example 46 claim 4) to distinguish claims that do not recite abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(I). If claim limitations are essentially mathematical relationships/formulas/calculations they may be an abstract idea under Prong One.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts that can be performed in the human mind, including observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(III). Claims reciting mental processes fall within the abstract idea grouping unless additional elements integrate them into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes fundamental economic principles or practices, commercial or legal interactions, and managing personal behavior, relationships, or interactions between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(II). These types of activities are grouped as abstract ideas for Step 2A Prong One analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One: Laws of nature / natural principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon (judicial exceptions other than abstract ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.04(b) for concepts and products courts have identified as laws of nature/natural phenomena. Use examples (e.g., Julitis Example 29; Controller for Injection Mold Example 45 claim 4) to assess whether a claimed limitation is a law of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One: Products of nature — Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim limitation is to a nature-based product, apply the MDC analysis to determine whether it is a product of nature judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2106.04(c). Consider whether changes in structure or function are more than minor/routine: examples include engineered antibodies (Example 16), inactivated/attenuated virus (Example 28), gel/granulated forms (Example 30); functional changes (rate of cell growth, immunogenic effect, taste, glycemic control) may demonstrate MDC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two: Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: If a judicial exception is recited, evaluate whether the additional claim elements integrate the exception into a practical application such that the claim is more than drafting to monopolize the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2106.04(d). Use considerations from case law, including "improvements to the functioning of a computer/other technology" and "particular treatment or prophylaxis." Integration requires that additional elements apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception to impose a meaningful limit on the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Significantly more / inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, amount to 'significantly more'—an inventive concept—beyond the recited judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2106.05 and 2106.05(a)-(h). Consider whether claimed additional elements are more than insignificant extra‑solution activity or well‑understood, routine, conventional activity; eligibility requires an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations distinguishing Prong Two vs. Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate Prong Two (integration into a practical application) from Step 2B (inventive concept): Prong Two asks whether additional elements meaningfully limit/use the exception; Step 2B asks whether those elements amount to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the court‑laid considerations (e.g., whether steps are merely data gathering, whether steps are conventional or merely instructions to apply a natural product) to determine where the claim falls. Examples: data gathering may be 'insignificant extra‑solution activity' (Example 45); a container that merely applies a natural product may not meaningfully limit the exception (Example 44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example-based indicators of eligibility or ineligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative fact-pattern outcomes indicate how the tests are applied: e.g., 'No exception recited → eligible at Step 2A Prong One'; 'additional limitation that does not meaningfully limit the claim → not integrated (Prong Two fails)'; 'mere data gathering or well‑known steps → not significantly more (Step 2B fails)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slides include 46 examples across technologies (biotech, pharmaceuticals, antibodies, vaccines, business methods, computer/software) showing eligible and ineligible claims consistent with case law (Example 39: facial detection – no exception recited; Example 44: denveric acid variations; Example 45: controller for injection mold demonstrates data gathering vs. integrated control). Consult the indexed examples to see which considerations were applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the MPEP examples and index as guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage the MPEP examples (1–46) and index to see how practical application and significantly‑more considerations were applied to a range of fact patterns and technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index indicates which examples provide a practical application or significantly more analysis and which considerations are evaluated in each example. Examples cover abstract ideas, life sciences, business methods, nature‑based products, and streamlined guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: DSMER pilot program: application eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for participation in the Deferred Subject Matter Eligibility Response (DSMER) pilot program: which applications are eligible and which are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligible: original non‑provisional utility application; does not claim benefit of an earlier‑filed U.S. non‑provisional (i.e., not a U.S. CON/DIV/CIP) — 371 or CON/DIV/CIP of PCT OK; claiming benefit to U.S. provisional or foreign‑filed application is OK. Ineligible: RCEs; applications with a First Action on the Merits (FAOM) already mailed; special cases (Track 1, Cancer Immunology, PPH, Petition to Make Special under MPEP 708.02). FAOM must include at least one SME rejection and at least one other rejection; SME rejection may be based on any steps of the SME analysis (MPEP 2106). Process is invitation‑based (examiner invites; applicant may elect to participate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural note: invitation and examination phases for DSMER
rubrics_metrics.description: The DSMER pilot is a two‑phase process: an invitation phase (examiner selects eligible applications and invites applicant) and an examination phase (applicant elects to participate and prosecution follows pilot parameters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant cannot initiate participation; both parties must agree for the application to enter the pilot. The pilot offers partial waiver of 37 CFR 1.111(b) so a response need not address the SME rejection to be compliant. See Federal Register Notice (87 FR 776) and USPTO DSMER webpage for details.
